results.result: During binocular rivalry with crossmodal cues, perceptual switches occurred rhythmically at ~8 Hz when cues matched the conscious percept and at ~3.5 Hz when cues mismatched the conscious percept. These rhythms were observed in behavioral data and were absent when cues were not task-relevant.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C23, C24, C48, C50 provide converging behavioral evidence from spectral analysis (Figure 3f) showing significant peaks at 7.5-8 Hz for matched cues (pcluster < 0.001) and 3.3-3.75 Hz for mismatched cues (pcluster < 0.001). Claims C25, C26, C52 demonstrate task-dependence through control conditions. The statistical rigor is appropriate with cluster-based permutation testing correcting for multiple comparisons. Claims C49, C51 appropriately contextualize findings within prior attentional sampling literature.

results.result: Attended low-frequency crossmodal cues significantly increased the probability of perceiving congruent visual images during binocular rivalry (0.68-3.97 s after cue onset), and this effect was mediated by attention as demonstrated by correlation between task performance and perceptual switching (r=0.46, p=0.006).
results.evaluation: Claims C37, C41, C42 present time-resolved behavioral effects with appropriate statistical testing (repeated measures ANOVA, FDR q=0.05, Figure 2). Claims C39, C40 provide critical evidence that effects depend on attention through correlation analysis between subjective reports and actual congruent cues. Claim C38 appropriately reports null effects across crossmodal cue types. The convergence of behavioral effects and attentional mediation strongly supports this result.

results.result: Mismatched cues induced stronger inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC) than matched cues at 3.5 Hz over right fronto-central-temporal electrodes [FT8, C6], and this 3.5 Hz ITPC positively correlated with perceptual switching across subjects for both mismatched (r=0.38, p=0.027) and matched (r=0.34, p=0.049) conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C53, C91 establish the EEG finding with appropriate spatial cluster-based statistics (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). Claims C55, C56 demonstrate brain-behavior correlations linking neural oscillations to perceptual outcomes. Claim C57 provides appropriate interpretation. The convergence of EEG differences and brain-behavior correlations, combined with rigorous cluster-based permutation testing (2000 shuffles, p<0.05 cluster-corrected), supports this neural correlate of divided attentional sampling.

results.result: Mismatched cues induced stronger ITPC than matched cues at 8 Hz over right parieto-occipital electrodes [P6, PO8], and 8 Hz ITPC was negatively correlated with perceptual switching during matched cues (r=-0.39, p=0.023), indicating that stronger 8 Hz phase coherence stabilized the current percept.
results.evaluation: Claims C54, C59 establish the EEG finding with cluster-based statistics (Figure 5a, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). Claim C58 appropriately reports the null correlation for mismatched cues. Claims C59, C60, C99 demonstrate the negative brain-behavior correlation for matched cues, with appropriate interpretation that increased 8 Hz coherence reduces switching. The selective correlation pattern (negative for matched, null for mismatched) and rigorous statistics support this as a neural correlate of focused attentional sampling.

results.result: At attentional sampling frequencies (3.5 Hz and 8 Hz), the strength of inter-trial phase coherence over fronto-temporal and parieto-occipital regions correlated with behaviorally reported changes in consciousness, providing novel evidence for attentional sampling during binocular rivalry in both behavior and EEG.
results.evaluation: This is a summary result integrating the behavioral rhythms (Result 1) with the neural correlates (Results 3-4). Claims C5, C61, C67, C68 synthesize the convergent evidence across behavioral and neural measures. The support comes from the combination of: (1) behavioral spectral peaks at predicted frequencies, (2) EEG phase coherence differences at those same frequencies, and (3) brain-behavior correlations linking neural oscillations to perceptual outcomes. This multi-level convergence strongly supports the main conclusion.

results.result: The rhythmic effects of attentional sampling on perceptual changes disappeared when cues were not task-relevant, confirming that perceptual changes depended on the allocation of attention and that attention can flexibly sample away from a conscious image in a task-dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C26, C70 establish the task-dependence through comparison of attended vs. non-attended conditions. Claims C86, C89, C90 provide specific evidence that periodic responses were absent outside attended cue periods (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Claim C87 provides appropriate interpretation. The control condition (non-attended cues showing no rhythmic effects) is critical for establishing that effects are attention-dependent rather than stimulus-driven, and this is well-demonstrated.

results.result: Compared to visual-only baseline, mismatched cues facilitated earlier first-switches (0.63-2.45 s and 3.78-6.87 s after cue onset), while matched cues delayed first-switches (1.27-3.77 s after onset), as shown by cumulative density function analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C44, C45 describe the opposing effects on switch timing, while C46, C47 provide specific time windows with appropriate statistics (paired t-tests, FDR q=0.05, Figure 3b). The cumulative density function analysis is an appropriate method for analyzing first-switch timing. The bidirectional effects (facilitation vs. delay) depending on match/mismatch condition strengthen the interpretation that cues actively modulate rivalry dynamics.

results.result: The observed ~3.5 Hz rhythm during mismatched cues is consistent with previous reports of divided attentional sampling between two locations, while the ~8 Hz rhythm during matched cues is consistent with focused attention to a single location, extending attentional sampling findings to binocular rivalry.
results.evaluation: Claims C64, C65, C66 appropriately contextualize the findings within prior attentional sampling literature (Fiebelkorn et al., 2013; Landau and Fries, 2012; Busch and VanRullen, 2010). Claims C83, C88, C97 provide interpretation extending these findings to binocular rivalry. The frequencies observed match theoretical predictions from the attentional sampling hypothesis, and the authors appropriately cite relevant prior work. The extension to binocular rivalry is novel and well-supported by the data.

results.result: The study replicated previous findings that crossmodal cues can cause switches to suppressed stimuli when mismatched with the current percept and increase maintenance of dominant images when matched.
results.evaluation: Claims C62, C63 describe replication of prior crossmodal effects (Dieter et al., 2015; Lunghi and Alais, 2015; Lunghi et al., 2014) shown in Figure 2. The replication is important for establishing the basic crossmodal effect before examining its temporal dynamics. The effects are well-demonstrated with appropriate statistics and serve as a foundation for the novel rhythmic findings.

results.result: The study employed 34 subjects who continuously reported visual consciousness during binocular rivalry with orthogonal sinusoidal gratings (4.5 Hz and 20 Hz contrast modulation) while 64-channel EEG was recorded. Crossmodal cues (auditory/tactile, 4.5 or 20 Hz) were presented intermittently with visual-only baseline periods.
results.evaluation: These claims describe the basic experimental design and are factual statements about methods. Claims C28, C29, C153-C156 describe participants and ethics. Claims C30-C36 describe stimuli and timing. The design is clearly described and appropriate for testing the hypotheses. Sample size (N=34) is reasonable for within-subjects EEG study. The use of visual-only baseline periods is appropriate for control comparisons.

results.result: The study's design is unique in operationalizing 'target-detection' as the first reported change in visual consciousness for continuously presented stimuli, resolved at 16.7 ms (60 Hz) from 500 ms to 2000 ms following cue onset, with spectral analysis applied to this time window.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 describes the unique aspect of the design compared to prior attentional sampling studies. Claims C211-C215 describe the specific analysis approach for first switches. The temporal resolution (60 Hz) is appropriate for detecting oscillations in the 3-8 Hz range. The 0.5-2 s analysis window is justified to avoid onset transients and ensure analysis during cue periods. This methodological innovation is well-described and appropriate.

results.result: Statistical significance of behavioral spectra was assessed using a two-stage procedure: first detecting significant frequencies (p<0.005 uncorrected) through non-parametric randomization (5000 shuffles), then applying cluster-based correction for multiple comparisons (requiring ≥2 neighboring frequencies, pcluster<0.05).
results.evaluation: Claims C216-C223 describe the statistical approach, which follows established methods (Landau and Fries, 2012; Maris and Oostenveld, 2007). The two-stage approach appropriately controls for multiple comparisons while maintaining sensitivity. The use of 5000 shuffles provides robust null distributions. The cluster criterion (≥2 neighboring frequencies) is reasonable for spectral data. This rigorous statistical approach strengthens confidence in the behavioral findings.

results.result: ITPC analysis used appropriate methods including trial equalization through downsampling with replacement (100 iterations), analysis of evoked ITPC (0-2 s vs. -2-0 s baseline), and two-stage cluster-based permutation testing (2000 shuffles) with spatial clustering criterion (≥2 neighboring electrodes, <3.5 cm apart, p<0.05 cluster-corrected).
results.evaluation: Claims C230-C246 comprehensively describe the ITPC analysis methods. The trial equalization procedure (C233-C234) appropriately addresses the bias in ITPC due to varying trial numbers. The two-stage spatial clustering approach (C237-C246) follows established methods (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007) and appropriately controls for multiple comparisons across electrodes. The methods are rigorous and well-justified, supporting confidence in the EEG findings.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that the observed oscillations may reflect fluctuations in perception or decision criterion, noting that recent studies show both sensitivity and response criterion exhibit oscillations in the theta/alpha band, and that the current paradigm cannot resolve this distinction.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C112 appropriately acknowledge a limitation of the study. The distinction between perceptual and decision-level oscillations is an important theoretical issue (Ho et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018; Iemi and Busch, 2018). The authors correctly note that their paradigm cannot resolve this and suggest signal detection theory approaches for future work. This honest acknowledgment of limitations is appropriate and does not undermine the main findings.

results.result: The authors propose two alternative interpretations for the 3.5 Hz rhythm: (1) divided attentional sampling between sensory modalities (crossmodal sampling hypothesis), or (2) divided sampling between dominant and suppressed visual images (conscious-nonconscious sampling hypothesis), suggesting future experiments to distinguish these possibilities.
results.evaluation: Claims C114, C115, C117, C130, C132 present two plausible alternative interpretations of the 3.5 Hz rhythm. Claims C150, C151 appropriately suggest future experiments to distinguish these hypotheses. While both interpretations are consistent with the data, the current experiment cannot definitively distinguish between them. The authors appropriately present this as an open question requiring future work. The uncertainty about mechanism does not undermine the core finding of rhythmic sampling, but prevents definitive mechanistic conclusions.

results.result: The lack of high-frequency (20 Hz) crossmodal effects may reflect either an upper limit on crossmodal integration (~4 Hz based on prior work) or differences in stimulus parameters (size, type) compared to prior studies that showed high-frequency effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C122 propose that the lack of high-frequency effects may reflect crossmodal integration limits (supported by citations to Fujisaki and Nishida, 2005; Vroomen and Keetels, 2010). Claims C123-C128 note that Lunghi et al., 2014 did show high-frequency effects with different stimuli (smaller, contrast-modulated noise patterns vs. larger, luminance-modulated gratings). Claims C126, C127 acknowledge that whether stimulus size affects crossmodal effects is unknown. The authors appropriately present multiple possible explanations but cannot definitively determine which is correct. This uncertainty is honestly acknowledged.

results.result: From the data alone, it cannot be inferred whether attention samples at 8 or 4 Hz during conventional binocular rivalry without crossmodal cues, with the authors suggesting that increased attention to stimulus competition may be required to observe attentional sampling rhythms.
results.evaluation: Claims C84, C85 appropriately acknowledge a limitation: the study only examined rivalry with crossmodal cues, not conventional rivalry. The suggestion that task-relevant attention may be necessary is consistent with the control condition showing no rhythms when cues were ignored (C86). This is an honest acknowledgment that the findings may not generalize to passive rivalry viewing, which is appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: The right fronto-temporal region showing 3.5 Hz effects differs from regions previously implicated in attentional sampling, possibly due to differences in paradigm (rivalry between overlapping stimuli vs. divided attention across hemifields) or lateralization of tactile input, requiring future experiments to characterize regional contributions.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C96 appropriately contextualize the regional findings within prior literature. Claims C102, C103 acknowledge that the right-lateralization may be due to left-lateralized tactile input and that future experiments controlling for lateralization are needed. The authors appropriately note that their paradigm differs from prior work (overlapping rivalry stimuli vs. spatially separated locations), which could explain regional differences. This honest discussion of regional specificity and need for future work is appropriate.

results.result: The 8 Hz parieto-occipital ITPC finding is consistent with prior work showing phase-dependent perception at ~7 Hz over fronto-central electrodes for focused attention, and with findings that right parieto-occipital theta/alpha oscillations modulate perception and may preferentially represent temporal information.
results.evaluation: Claims C100, C101 cite prior work on phase-dependent perception (Busch et al., 2009; Busch and VanRullen, 2010). Claims C105, C106 cite work on parieto-occipital theta/alpha in attention and bistable perception (van Driel et al., 2014; Ronconi et al., 2017). Claim C107 provides interpretation consistent with right-parietal temporal processing (Battelli et al., 2007; Guggisberg et al., 2011). The contextualization within prior literature is appropriate and strengthens the interpretation of the parieto-occipital findings.

results.result: The attentional sampling hypothesis, supported by prior literature, suggests that attention rhythmically enhances sensory processing at ~8 Hz for single objects and ~4 Hz for multiple objects, with neural evidence showing target detection depends on pre-target phase of ~7-8 Hz oscillations.
